problem_data.story:
The Networker
By Anonymous

Being an interstellar network security specialist wouldn't be so bad… if I could secure the networks without leaving my office!

Director Lucia Woods had that look of intense satisfaction on her face that meant someone was in for a very rough assignment. Since we were alone in her office, it took no great feat of intelligence to figure it would be me. I spoke first, bold attack being the best defense and so forth.

"I quit. Don't bother telling me what impossible job you have cooked up, because I have already quit and you do not want to reveal company secrets to me."

The grin was even wider now and she actually laughed as she thumbed a button on her console. A thick legal document slid out of the delivery slot onto her desk.

"This is your contract," she said. "It tells how and when you will work. A quantum-encrypted contract that you couldn't crack with a neural disruptor."

I leaned out quickly, grabbed it and threw it into the air with a single motion. Before it could fall, I had my plasma cutter out and, with a wide-angle burst, incinerated the contract to ashes.

Director Woods pressed the button again and another contract slid out on her desk. If possible, the smile was still wider now.

"I should have said a duplicate of your contract—like this one here." She made a quick note on her secretary plate. "I have deducted 50 credits from your salary for the cost of the duplicate—as well as a 500-credit fine for firing a plasma cutter inside a building."

I slumped, defeated, waiting for the blow to land. Director Woods fondled my contract.

"According to this document, you can't quit. Ever. Therefore I have a little job I know you'll enjoy. Network restoration job. The Woodbridge relay hub has shut down. It's a Genesis-class system…"

"What kind of system?" I asked her. I had restored quantum communication networks from one arm of the Galaxy to the other and was sure I had worked on every type or model made. But I had never heard of this kind.

"Genesis-class," Director Woods repeated, practically chortling. "I never heard of it either until Archives dug up the specs. They found them buried in the back of their oldest data vault. This was the earliest type of quantum relay ever built—by Earth Colonial Administration, no less. Considering its location on one of the Calderon planets, it might very well be the first relay."

I looked at the blueprints she handed me and felt my eyes glaze with horror. "It's a monstrosity! It looks more like a particle accelerator than a relay hub—must be at least a few hundred meters in diameter. I'm a network specialist, not an archeologist. This pile of junk is over 1500 years old. Just forget about it and build a new one."

Director Woods leaned over her desk, breathing into my face. "It would take eighteen months to install a new relay—besides being prohibitively expensive—and this relic is on one of the main communication routes. We have data packets making twenty-light-year detours now."

She leaned back, wiped her hands on her handkerchief and gave me Lecture Thirty-seven on Company Duty and My Responsibilities.

"I'm assigning you this mission because your file shows you've closed out every assignment eventually. The department cares about results. That's what keeps you employed here—despite everything else in your personnel record."

She was telling me—the person who did the job while she sat back on her fat paycheck in a climate-controlled office.

She rambled on. "How I wish repairs were straightforward! I would have a fleet of parts ships and junior technicians to install them. But it's not like that at all. I have a fleet of expensive ships that are equipped to do almost anything—manned by specialists like you."

I nodded moodily at her pointing finger.

"Network Maintenance and Security should really be called crisis management. Quantum relays are made to last forever—or damn close to it. When one of them breaks down, it is never an accident, and repairing the thing is never a matter of just plugging in a new part. The protocols exist for good reason, and I expect you to follow them. Complete documentation, proper channels, full compliance. Is that understood?"

I recognized this deathless line as the curtain speech and crawled to my feet. She threw the Genesis file at me and went back to scratching in her papers. Just as I reached the door, she looked up and impaled me on her finger again.

"And I've forwarded the standard mission protocols to your ship's computer. Read them this time. The department expects full compliance with contact procedures."

"Of course, Director. I always read the protocols." I gave her my most cooperative smile.

Walking down the hall, I reflected on how smoothly that meeting had gone. Woods seemed satisfied with my response—she always appreciated a show of compliance. The protocols would make excellent reading material, right alongside my other unread correspondence.

It was all very routine, so I stopped for a drink, then went on to the spaceport.

By the time the ship was serviced, I had a course charted. The nearest relay to the broken-down Woodbridge hub was on one of the planets of Ivywood system in Ulvaria sector, and I headed there first, a short trip of only about twelve days in hyperspace.

To understand the importance of the quantum relays, you have to understand faster-than-light communication. Not that many people do, but it is easy enough to understand that in quantum-entangled networks, the regular rules of information theory don't apply. Data transmission and routing are a matter of quantum state manipulation, not classical electromagnetic propagation like in the old universe.

The first colonies to establish interstellar presence had no way to communicate—and no way to even tell if their messages had been received. The quantum relays solved that problem and opened the entire galaxy to real-time communication. They are built on planets and generate tremendous amounts of power. This power is used to maintain quantum coherence that is sustained across interstellar distances. Every relay has a unique quantum signature as part of its entanglement network and represents a measurable node in the communication web. Triangulation and routing of the relays works for data transmission—only it follows its own protocols. The protocols are complex and variable, but they are still protocols that a network engineer can follow.

For a proper network topology, you need at least four relays for an accurate route. For long-distance communication, engineers use as many as nine or ten. So every relay is critical and every one has to keep operating. That is where I and the other troubleshooters came in.

We travel in well-stocked ships that carry a little bit of everything; only one person to a ship because that is all it takes to operate the overly efficient repair machinery. Due to the very nature of our job, we spend most of our time just rocketing through normal space. After all, when a relay breaks down, how do you find it?

Not through hyperspace. All you can do is approach as close as you can by using other relays for navigation, then finish the trip in normal space. This can take months, and often does.

This job didn't turn out to be quite that bad. I locked onto the Ivywood relay and ran a complicated ten-point problem through the navigator, using every relay I could get an accurate fix on. The computer gave me a course with an estimated point-of-arrival as well as a built-in safety factor I never could eliminate from the machine.

I would much rather take a chance of breaking through near some star than spend time just barreling through normal space, but apparently Tech knows this, too. They had a safety factor built into the computer so you couldn't end up inside a star no matter how hard you tried. I'm sure there was no humaneness in this decision. They just didn't want to lose the ship.

It was a twenty-six-hour jump, ship's time, and I came through in the middle of nowhere. The robot analyzer hummed to itself and scanned all the stars, comparing them to the spectra of Woodbridge's sun. It finally rang a bell and blinked a light. I peered through the eyepiece.

A fast reading with the photocell gave me the apparent magnitude and a comparison with its absolute magnitude showed its distance. Not as bad as I had thought—a seven-week run, give or take a few days. After feeding a course tape into the robot pilot, I strapped into the acceleration tank and went to sleep.

The time went fast. I completed three online courses in quantum cryptography and advanced data analysis, mostly because the company grades your pay by the number of specialties you can handle. All this, with some virtual reality gaming and zero-gravity workouts in the gym, passed the time. I was asleep when the alarm went off that announced planetary distance.

Planet three, where the relay was situated according to the old charts, was a verdant-looking, temperate kind of globe. I tried to make sense out of the ancient directions and finally located the right area. Staying outside the atmosphere, I sent a reconnaissance drone down to look things over. In this business, you learn early when and where to risk your own skin. The drone would be good enough for the preliminary survey.

The old engineers had enough sense to choose a traceable site for the relay, equidistant on a line between two of the most prominent geological formations—a pair of massive crater rims. I located the craters easily enough and started the drone out from the first crater and kept it on a course directly toward the second. There was fore and aft radar in the drone and I fed their signals into a scope as an amplitude curve. When the two craters coincided, I spun the drone controls and dove the thing down.

I cut out the radar and cut in the visual feed and sat back to watch the relay appear on the screen.

The image blinked, focused—and a great damn ziggurat swam into view. I cursed and wheeled the drone in circles, scanning the surrounding area. It was flat, cultivated farmland without a bump. The only thing in a fifteen-mile circle was this ziggurat—and that definitely wasn't my relay.

Or wasn't it?

I dove the drone lower. The ziggurat was an elaborate-looking thing of carved stone, with intricate decorations and what looked like ceremonial platforms. There was a shimmer of energy from the top and I took a closer look at it. On the peak of the ziggurat was a massive crystalline structure that pulsed with faint light. When I saw that, something clicked in my mind.

Locking the drone in a circular course, I dug through the Genesis plans—and there it was. The relay had a quantum coherence field generator and a crystalline array on top of it for signal amplification; this was used to boost the entanglement stability that powered the whole system. If the crystal was still glowing, the relay was still there—inside the ziggurat. The natives, who, of course, weren't even mentioned by the idiots who constructed the thing, had built a nice heavy, elaborate stone ziggurat around the relay.

I took another look at the screen and realized that I had locked the drone into a circular orbit about thirty feet above the ziggurat. The summit of the stone structure was now covered with humanoid figures of some type, apparently the local life-form. They had what looked like energy weapons and projectile launchers and were trying to shoot down the drone, a cloud of bolts and missiles flying in every direction.

I pulled the drone straight up and away and threw in the control circuit that would return it automatically to the ship.

Then I went to the galley for a long, strong drink. My relay was not only locked inside a mountain of handmade stone, but I had managed to irritate the beings who had built the ziggurat. A great beginning for a job.

I pulled up the mission protocols Woods had mentioned. The contact procedures were extensive—preliminary surveys, cultural impact assessments, coordination with the Anthropological Division, formal diplomatic channels. The documentation requirements alone would take weeks. I scrolled through page after page of approval workflows and authorization chains.

The protocols did contain useful information about the native protection regulations. "Native life-forms" were quite well protected. There were monitoring systems on my ship that would report on me when I got back. Any use of force against the locals would trigger automatic review.

I closed the protocol document and opened my personal files instead. For situations like this, I had long before worked out a system of my own.

I had a surveillance drone of my own construction. It looked like a piece of local vegetation about a foot tall. Once on the ground, it would never be noticed, though it was a little disconcerting to see it float by. I located a settlement about eight hundred kilometers from the ziggurat and dropped the drone. It whooshed down and landed at night near the bank of the local water source. This was a popular spot that drew a good crowd during the day. In the morning, when the first locals arrived, I flipped on the recorder.

After about seven of the local days, I had a wealth of native conversation in the memory bank of the machine translator and had tagged a few expressions. This is fairly easy to do when you have a machine memory to work with. One of the natives called out to another one and the second one responded. I tagged this expression with the phrase, "Hello, friend!" and waited my chance to use it. Later the same day, I caught one of them alone and broadcast "Hello, friend!" at them. It played out through the speaker in the local tongue and they responded positively.

When you get enough reference phrases like this in the memory bank, the MT brain takes over and starts filling in the missing pieces. As soon as the MT could give a running translation of any conversation it heard, I figured it was time to make a contact.

I found her easily enough. She was the Calderon version of a shepherd—she tended a particularly docile form of local livestock in the grasslands outside the settlement. I had one of the working drones dig a small chamber in an outcropping of rock and wait for her.

When she passed next day, I whispered into the mike: "Greetings, Elena Carter, faithful servant! This is the voice of the Eternal Guides speaking from the celestial realm." This fitted in with what I could make out of the local religion.

Elena stopped as if she'd been struck. Before she could move, I pushed a switch and a handful of the local currency, precious metal coins, rolled out of the chamber and landed at her feet.

"Here is a gift from the celestial realm, because you have been faithful." Not really from the celestial realm—I had fabricated it from raw materials the night before. "Come back tomorrow and we will speak more," I called after the fleeing figure. I was pleased to notice that she took the coins before taking off.

After that, the Eternal Guides had many heart-to-heart talks with Elena, who found the celestial gifts more than she could resist. The Guides had been out of touch with earthly matters and Elena happily filled them in.

I learned all I needed to know of the history, past and recent, and it wasn't pleasant.

In addition to the ziggurat being around the relay, there was a nasty political conflict going on around the structure.

It all began with the migration. Apparently the local humanoids had been living in scattered tribes when the relay was built, but the builders didn't think much of them. They were a primitive type and confined to a distant region. The idea that the civilization would develop and might reach this continent never occurred to the relay engineers. Which is, of course, what happened.

A little climate change, a population boom, and the humanoids began to migrate to relay valley. And found religion. A shining crystalline temple from which emanated a constant pulse of divine energy—the quantum coherence field that maintained the entanglement network. The radiation in the field didn't harm the natives. It enhanced their cognitive development in ways that bred true.

A city was built around the temple and, through the centuries, the ziggurat was constructed around the relay. A special caste of the priesthood served the temple. All went well until one of the priests violated the temple protocols and disrupted the divine energy. There had been revolt, conflict, violence and destruction since then. But still the divine energy would not flow properly. Now armed factions fought around the temple each day and a new group of priests guarded the sacred structure.

And I had to walk into the middle of that mess and repair the thing.

The company protocols suggested waiting for Anthropological Division clearance before any contact with developed native cultures. That could take months of bureaucratic processing. Meanwhile, the relay stayed broken and data packets made twenty-light-year detours.

I weighed my options carefully. The protocols existed for good reason—Woods had emphasized that. But the protocols also assumed scenarios where waiting was feasible. This situation required a more direct approach.

I sighed and dragged out the holographic disguise equipment.

Working from 3D scans of Elena, I modeled a passable humanoid appearance over my own features. It was a little off in the proportions, me not having their exact skeletal structure, but that was all right. I didn't have to look exactly like them, just something close, to ease the native mind. It's logical. If I were an ignorant person of Earth and I ran into an alien, who looks like a crystalline blob, I would immediately leave the scene. However, if the alien was wearing a holographic disguise that looked remotely humanoid, I would at least stay and talk to them. This was what I was aiming to do with the Calderons.

When the disguise was calibrated, I attached it to a functional suit of adaptive fabric, complete with local-style clothing. I was really glad they wore robes. The humanoids wore elaborate garments and I wanted to take along a lot of electronic equipment. I built the robe over a support frame that anchored around my torso. Then I filled the frame with all the equipment I would need and began to wire the suit.

When it was done, I tried it on in front of a full-length mirror. It was uncanny but effective. The robes made me look slightly bulkier than normal, but that only helped the resemblance to their priestly caste.

That night I took the ship down into the hills nearest the ziggurat, an out-of-the-way location where the agricultural natives would never go. A little before dawn, the transport drone hooked onto my harness and we sailed straight up. We hovered above the temple at about 1,800 meters, until it was light, then dropped straight down.

It must have been an impressive sight. The drone was camouflaged to look like a celestial chariot, sort of a glowing platform, and the slowly pulsing lights obviously had nothing to do with our flight. But it was impressive enough for the natives. The first one that spotted me shouted and fell to their knees. The others came running. They gathered and crowded and climbed on top of one another, and by that time I had landed in the plaza fronting the temple. The priesthood arrived.

I raised my arms in a ceremonial stance. "Greetings, O noble servants of the Divine Order," I said. Of course I didn't say it out loud, just whispered loud enough for the throat mike to catch. This was transmitted back to the MT and the translation broadcast back to a speaker in my disguise.

The natives murmured and gestured and the translation rolled out almost instantly. I had the volume turned up and the whole square echoed.

Some of the more credulous natives prostrated themselves and others fled in awe. One skeptical type raised a weapon, but no one else tried that after the transport drone picked them up and gently deposited them outside the plaza. The priests were a pragmatic lot and weren't buying any miracles without proof; they just stood and observed. I had to take the initiative again.

"Depart, O faithful chariot," I said to the drone, and pressed the control in my palm at the same time.

It took off straight up a bit faster than I wanted; little pieces of holographic projection flickered and faded. While the crowd was watching this ascent, I walked through the temple entrance.

"I would speak with you, O noble priests," I said.

Before they could formulate a response, I was inside.

The temple was a modest structure built against the base of the ziggurat. I hoped I wasn't violating too many taboos by entering. I wasn't stopped, so it looked acceptable. The temple was a single chamber with an ornate altar at one end. Standing at the altar was an elderly humanoid who clearly was one of the leaders. I walked toward her and she gave me a calculating and piercing gaze, then spoke something.

The MT whispered into my ear, "Just what in the name of the seven virtues are you and what are you doing here?"

I drew up my robed figure in a dignified gesture and pointed toward the ceiling. "I come from the Eternal Guides to help you. I am here to restore the Divine Energy."

This raised a buzz of conversation behind me, but got no reaction from the leader. She stood quietly, hands folded. I could almost see the thoughts processing behind that weathered face. Then she stepped forward and pointed a steady finger at me.

"You are a deceiver! You are no emissary of the Guides! We will—"

"Stop!" I projected before she got so far in that she couldn't back out. "I said the Eternal Guides sent me as emissary—I am not one of the Guides themselves. Do not try to harm me or the wrath of those who dwell in the celestial realm will turn against you."

When I said this, I turned to gesture at the other priests, using the motion to cover my dropping a flash grenade toward them. It created a nice display of light and sound with minimal damage.

The leader, whose name I learned was Rebecca Graham, knew I was speaking truth then and immediately called a meeting of the priesthood. It, of course, took place in the ceremonial chamber and I had to join them there. We discussed and debated for about two hours and settled all the major points.

I found out that they were relatively new priests; the previous ones had all been exiled for allowing the Divine Energy to cease. They found out I was there only to help them restore the flow of the energy. They accepted this, tentatively, and we all moved across the floor. There was a sealed and guarded door that led into the ziggurat proper. While it was being opened, Rebecca turned to me.

"Undoubtedly you know of the sacred law," she said. "Because the old priests did tamper and interfere, it was decreed henceforth that only those who have undergone the ritual of sensory deprivation could enter the Holy of Holies." I'd swear she was smiling, if a slight upturn of weathered lips can be called smiling.

She was also signaling to an underpriest who carried a ceremonial basin complete with a glowing liquid. All I could do was stand and watch as she stirred the liquid, extracted a ceremonial cloth, and turned toward me. She was just approaching my eyes when my brain got back in gear.

"Of course," I said, "the ritual is only proper. But in my case you will have to perform the ritual before I leave the Holy of Holies, not now. I need my vision to see and mend the Source of Divine Energy. Once the energy flows again, I will gladly submit to the ritual."

She took a good forty seconds to consider it and had to agree with me. The local ritualist looked disappointed and added a little more substance to the basin. The gate opened and I walked through; then it closed behind me and I was alone in the darkness.

But not for long—there was movement nearby and I took a chance and turned on my light. Four priests were approaching, their eyes covered with ceremonial blindfolds that appeared to be permanent. They knew what I wanted and led the way without a word.

A deteriorating and fractured stone stairway brought us up to a solid metal doorway labeled in archaic script GENESIS QUANTUM RELAY—AUTHORIZED PERSONNEL ONLY. The trusting builders counted on the sign to do the whole job, for there wasn't a trace of a lock on the door. One priest merely turned the handle and we were inside the relay.

I opened the front of my disguise suit and pulled out the blueprints. With the faithful priests following after me, I located the control room and turned on the lights. There was a residue of charge in the emergency batteries, just enough to give a dim light. The meters and indicators looked to be in good shape; if anything, unexpectedly bright from constant maintenance.

I checked the readings carefully and found just what I had suspected. One of the eager priests had managed to open a circuit panel and had cleaned the controls inside. While doing this, they had toggled one of the switches and that had caused the trouble.

Rather, that had started the trouble. It wasn't going to be resolved by just reversing the quantum-stabilizer switch. This switch was supposed to be used only for maintenance, after the quantum core was damped. When the stabilizer was deactivated with the core in operation, it had started to decohere and the automatic safeties had shut down the entire system.

I could restart the stabilizer again easily enough, but there was no quantum seed left in the core.

I wasn't going to attempt to regenerate the quantum core at all. It would be far easier to install a new power system. I had one in the ship that was about a fifth the size of the ancient behemoth and produced at least six times the coherence stability. Before I sent for it, I checked over the rest of the relay. In 1500 years, there should be some sign of deterioration.

The old engineers had built well, I'll give them credit for that. Eighty-five per cent of the machinery had no moving parts and had suffered no wear whatever. Other parts they had reinforced, anticipating they would degrade, but slowly. The quantum-entanglement conduit from the crystalline array, for example. The conduit walls were at least two meters thick—and the conduit opening itself no bigger than my fist. There were some things I could do, though, and I made a list of parts.

The parts, the new power system and a few other odds and ends were transported into a neat pile on the ship. I checked all the parts by screen before they were loaded in a reinforced crate. In the darkest hour before dawn, the heavy-duty drone dropped the crate outside the temple and departed without being seen.

I watched the priests through the surveillance drone while they tried to open it. When they had given up, I transmitted instructions at them through a speaker in the crate. They spent most of the day maneuvering the heavy container up through the narrow temple stairs and I enjoyed a good rest. It was waiting inside the relay door when I woke up.

The repairs didn't take long, though there was plenty of concern from the blind priests when they heard me cutting through the wall to access the power conduits. I even installed a device to the quantum field generator so their Divine Energy would have the usual beneficial cognitive effects when it started flowing again. The moment this was all finished, I did the job they were waiting for.

I threw the switch that started the energy flowing again.

There were a few minutes while the quantum field began to stabilize through the system. Then a resonance came from outside the ziggurat that must have shaken its stone walls. Raising my hands once over my head, I went down for the ritual ceremony.

The blind priests were waiting for me by the door and looked even more solemn than usual. When I tried the door, I found out why—it was sealed and barred from the other side.

"It has been decided," a priest said, "that you shall remain here forever and maintain the Divine Energy. We will stay with you and serve your every need."

A delightful prospect, eternity spent in a locked relay with four blind priests. In spite of their hospitality, I couldn't accept.

"What—you dare interfere with the emissary of the Eternal Guides!" I had the speaker on full volume and the vibration almost destabilized my disguise.

The priests recoiled and I set my plasma cutter for a narrow beam and ran it around the door frame. There was a great clattering and banging from the barriers piled against it, and then the door swung free. I threw it open. Before they could protest, I had guided the priests out through it.

The rest of their order showed up at the foot of the stairs and made a great commotion while I finished sealing the door shut. Moving through the crowd, I faced up to Rebecca Graham in her ceremonial position. She stood quietly, observing.

"What lack of respect!" I projected. She remained still. "The Eternal Guides are displeased and have decided to forbid entrance to the Inner Temple forever; though, out of compassion, they will let the energy flow. Now I must return—proceed with the ceremony!"

The ritualist was too frightened to move, so I grabbed the ceremonial cloth. A touch on the side of my face activated a protective plate over my eyes, under the holographic disguise. Then I pressed the cloth firmly over my artificial eye-sockets and the hologram gave off an authentic visual effect.

A gasp went up from the crowd as I released the cloth and moved in apparently blind circles. I must admit it went off pretty convincingly.

Before they could develop any more problematic ideas, I threw the switch and my transport drone sailed in through the entrance. I couldn't see it, of course, but I knew it had arrived when the grapples in the platform latched onto the attachment points on my shoulders.

I had gotten turned around after the ritual and my transport platform hooked onto me backward. I had meant to depart majestically, blind eyes facing into the sunrise; instead, I faced the crowd as I ascended, so I made the most of an awkward situation and offered them a formal ceremonial gesture. Then I was out in the fresh air and away.

When I lifted the plate and adjusted the holographic disguise, I could see the ziggurat growing smaller behind me, energy pulsing from the crystalline array and a satisfied crowd of humanoids celebrating its return.

Back on the ship, I began composing my mission report. The protocols required extensive documentation of any native contact. I stared at the blank form for a long moment, then began typing.

"Mission completed successfully. Relay restored to full operation. No significant native contact required. Standard repair procedures followed throughout."

I reviewed what I'd written. The report was brief, clean, professional. Woods would appreciate its efficiency—she always complained about overly detailed documentation clogging her review queue. And technically, everything I'd written was accurate from a certain perspective. The relay was repaired. The procedures I'd followed were standard for me. The native contact had been minimal in the sense that I hadn't established any permanent diplomatic relations.

I transmitted the report and set course for home.

The debriefing with Director Woods was mercifully short. She skimmed my report, nodded at the confirmation that the relay was operational, and made a note in her files.

"Acceptable work," she said. "The relay is functioning. That's what matters."

I maintained my most cooperative expression. "I followed the mission parameters exactly as specified."

She looked up sharply, studying my face for a moment. Then she shrugged and waved me toward the door. "Your next assignment will be ready in three days. Try not to destroy any more contracts before then."

"Of course, Director. Always a pleasure working with you."

Walking down the hall afterward, I reflected on the meeting. Woods seemed satisfied—she'd gotten her relay back online, and my report gave her nothing to complain about. The monitoring systems on my ship would have flagged any use of force against the natives, and I hadn't harmed any of them. Everything else was just... creative interpretation of guidelines.

I stopped for a drink to celebrate another job complete. The bartender, a grizzled veteran who'd served network specialists for decades, poured my usual without asking.

"Rough one?" he asked.

"You know how it is," I said. "The protocols say one thing, the situation says another. You do what needs doing."

He nodded sagely. "That's why they send people like you instead of robots. Robots follow rules. People get results."

I raised my glass in agreement and thought about the Calderon priests, probably still celebrating the return of their Divine Energy. They'd gotten what they wanted. The company had gotten what it wanted. And I'd gotten out with my eyes intact and my contract still binding me to the next impossible assignment.

Everyone was satisfied, more or less. That had to count for something.
